metadata.title: What drives the performance of Chinese urban and rural secondary schools: A machine learning approach using PISA 2018

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 micro-level data for China, focusing on school-level average outcomes for mathematics, science, and reading. The analytic sample is restricted to four eastern provinces (Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, Zhejiang) and further excludes schools with insufficient information; student-level information is then weighted-averaged to match school-level data. The manuscript does not report the specific PISA student weight variable name or whether complex-sampling replicate weights were applied in the ML training/evaluation. Because the paper applies linear regression and XGBoost and then uses Shapley flow for feature attribution, it is unclear whether survey weights were incorporated into model fitting; analysts should verify in the original PISA data documentation whether weights were used and, if not, interpret results as descriptive/predictive rather than fully population-representative.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper does not describe any missing-data strategy (e.g., complete-case exclusion, imputation, or PV-specific handling) beyond excluding schools with insufficient information. Given that PISA datasets typically contain missing questionnaire responses and that the study uses many background and intermediate learning variables, the absence of a documented missing-data procedure is a reporting gap that affects reproducibility and may bias estimates if missingness is systematic.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Uses PISA 2018 micro-level data for China, restricted to students from Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, and Zhejiang. Excludes schools with insufficient information. The outcome is constructed as the school-level average score across mathematics, science, and reading; student-level characteristics are weighted-averaged to the school level and matched to school-level data. The study then defines 'best' and 'worst' schools within urban and rural areas based on the highest vs. lowest school-level PISA average scores.

confounders_identified.variable_name: Two or more schools in area

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 China (Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, Zhejiang) — school-level average of mathematics, science, and reading (urban best vs benchmark)
main_findings.target_variable: School academic performance (best urban school vs benchmark)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Linear regression outperforms XGBoost (exact accuracy/R² not reported). Shapley flow benchmark difference: METASPAM contributes +41.96 points; grade repetition contributes −23.02 points (reported for worst urban).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 China the study leveraged meta-cognition (METASPAM), class size (CLSIZE), and socioeconomic status (ESCS) (with intermediate pathways via competitiveness perception, PERCOMP) to predict school academic performance for the best urban schools versus a benchmark school, finding that intermediate learning outcomes and student characteristics positively contribute to higher scores. This indicates that strengthening students’ credibility-assessment meta-cognition and improving family socioeconomic and learning conditions may narrow urban school performance gaps, though the study’s attribution is based on Shapley flow rather than a fully identified causal effect.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 China (Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, Zhejiang) — school-level average of mathematics, science, and reading (urban worst vs benchmark)
main_findings.target_variable: School academic performance (worst urban school vs benchmark)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Linear regression outperforms XGBoost (exact accuracy/R² not reported). Shapley flow benchmark difference: grade repetition (REPEAT) contributes −23.02 points; intermediate learning outcomes and student characteristics are described as negative contributors.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 China the study leveraged grade repetition (REPEAT), socioeconomic status (ESCS), learning time (TMINS), parental emotional support (EMOSUPS), and expected occupational status (BSMJ) to predict school academic performance for the worst urban schools versus a benchmark school, finding that poorer intermediate learning outcomes and weaker student characteristics reduce achievement. This indicates that urban policy should prioritize reducing grade repetition and supporting families’ emotional and learning resources to improve intermediate learning outcomes, while recognizing that the paper does not report a full set of predictive performance metrics and uses Shapley-based feature attribution.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 China (Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, Zhejiang) — school-level average of mathematics, science, and reading (best rural vs benchmark)
main_findings.target_variable: School academic performance (best rural school vs benchmark)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Linear regression outperforms XGBoost (exact accuracy/R² not reported). Directional Shapley flow results reported: ICT resources at home (ICTRES) worsen rural best performance relative to benchmark, while computer availability in school (RATCMP1) compensates; admission policies (ADMISSION) yield higher scores than benchmark.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 China the study leveraged school ICT availability (RATCMP1), learning-environment quality (STUBEHA), and admission policy complexity (ADMISSION) (counteracting home ICT constraints, ICTRES) to predict school academic performance for the best rural schools versus a benchmark school, finding that rural school characteristics play a larger role than in urban areas. This indicates that rural achievement improvement may depend more on school-level resource provision and learning-environment quality (including ICT access), though the study’s evidence is based on predictive modeling with Shapley flow rather than randomized causal identification.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 China (Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, Zhejiang) — school-level average of mathematics, science, and reading (worst rural vs benchmark)
main_findings.target_variable: School academic performance (worst rural school vs benchmark)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Linear regression outperforms XGBoost (exact accuracy/R² not reported). Directional Shapley flow results reported: ESCS, TMINS, and EMOSUPS negatively affect intermediate learning outcomes and academic performance; ICTRES is negative; RATCMP1 is negative for the worst rural school relative to benchmark.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 China the study leveraged socioeconomic status (ESCS), learning time (TMINS), parental emotional support (EMOSUPS), and ICT resources (ICTRES and RATCMP1) to predict school academic performance for the worst rural schools versus a benchmark school, finding that both family-related factors and ICT constraints depress intermediate learning outcomes and achievement. This indicates that rural policy should combine family-support interventions with targeted subsidies for ICT resources at both home and school, while noting that the paper does not provide full predictive accuracy metrics and uses Shapley flow for feature attribution.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2018 micro-level data for China, restricted to students from Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, and Zhejiang, and constructs a school-level outcome as the average of mathematics, science, and reading scores. After excluding schools with insufficient information, student characteristics are weighted-averaged to the school level, and schools are compared as “best” vs “worst” within urban and rural categories (urban defined by population threshold). The authors fit linear regression and XGBoost models on the school-level features and report that linear regression outperforms XGBoost, but they do not provide standard predictive metrics (e.g., R²/accuracy) in the text. They then use Shapley flow to estimate feature contributions relative to a benchmark school (581 points), finding that intermediate learning outcomes and student characteristics drive best–worst gaps in urban areas, while rural gaps are more sensitive to school characteristics, especially ICT resources. Limitations include missing-data handling not being documented and Shapley-based attribution being interpreted as causal structure without explicit causal identification assumptions.
